title: Piedmont Airlines 22

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Midair Collision between Piedmont Airlines Flight 22 and Lanseair Cessna 310

summary: A Piedmont Airlines Boeing 727 collided with a Lanseair Cessna 310 at 6,132 feet over Hendersonville, North Carolina. The Cessna deviated significantly from its assigned IFR clearance, proceeding on a southwesterly course instead of heading to the Asheville radio beacon as cleared. Both aircraft were destroyed and all 85 occupants were killed.
probable_cause: The Safety Board determines that the probable cause of this accident was the deviation of the Cessna from its IFR clearance resulting in a flightpath into airspace allocated to the Piedmont Boeing 727. The reason for such deviation cannot be specifically or positively identified. The minimum control procedures utilized by the FAA in the handling of the Cessna were a contributing factor. (p. 48)

factors.evidence: Asheville Approach Control did not specify the type of approach to be used at initial contact, and the clearance to proceed from VOR to Asheville RBN did not conform to recommended phraseology in ATP7110.1B, reducing precision and creating potential for misunderstanding (p. 30-31, 33)
Approach Control did not monitor Cessna's progress and did not alert the crew when they deviated from the assigned clearance; no surveillance radar was available at Asheville (p. 26, 46)
Cessna pilot may have had inadequate knowledge of the Asheville area and poor flight planning; crew anticipated ILS approach and became confused by ADF-2 clearance (p. 27, 43)
At 1201:18, the 727 collided with Cessna at 6,132 feet; Cessna impacted fuselage just aft of 727 cockpit; both aircraft destroyed in collision and impact forces (p. 5, 9)
After collision, 727 continued briefly then nosed over and fell rapidly to ground in disintegration (p. 9)

events.text: Atlanta Center advises Cessna N3121S to expect ILS approach at Asheville (p. 28)
Asheville Approach Control clears Cessna: cleared over VOR to Asheville radio beacon, maintain 7000 feet, report passing VOR (p. 7)
Cessna pilot acknowledges clearance with "Three two one Sierra" (p. 7)
Piedmont Flight 22 (Boeing 727 N68650) begins takeoff from Runway 16 at Asheville on IFR flight to Roanoke (p. 8)
Cessna reports position: "Two one Sierra just passed over the VOR, we're headed for Asheville now" (p. 9)
Asheville Tower clears Piedmont 22 to climb unrestricted to VOR, report passing VOR (p. 9)
Approach Control clears Cessna for ADF-2 approach to Runway 16, report Asheville radio beacon inbound (p. 9)
Boeing 727 and Cessna collide at 6,132 feet altitude, 9 miles southwest of Asheville VOR on 243° radial; Cessna impacts 727 fuselage just aft of cockpit; both aircraft destroyed (p. 5, 9)
All 82 aboard Piedmont 22 (5 crew, 74 passengers) and all 3 aboard Cessna killed; Boeing 727 crashes near Hendersonville, NC at Camp Pinewood (p. 5, 10)

recommendations.text: Review and modify aeronautical chart displays to include pictorial display of all navigational aids and fixes applicable to the approach, including depiction of Asheville RBN on ILS approach chart for missed-approach procedures (p. 49)
Expedite increases in ATC radar coverage in terminal areas as economics of money and manpower allow (p. 49)
Improve communication methods and procedures for IFR aircraft in non-radar environments; study feasibility of mandatory clearance readbacks by pilots (p. 49-50)
Revise recommended controller phraseology to provide specific instructions regarding clearances that affect flightpath changes (p. 50)
Increase frequency of monitoring aircraft progress in non-radar terminal areas through appropriate ATC communications (p. 50)
Review minimum levels of skill required for instrument pilot rating and evaluate against present system proficiency requisites (p. 50)
Establish requirement for annual proficiency flight check for all instrument-rated pilots utilizing the IFR system to ensure continued proficiency (p. 50)

safety_changes: Modified aeronautical chart displays to show all navigational aids and fixes used in approach procedures
Enhanced ATC communication procedures and phraseology for non-radar terminal areas
Increased emphasis on instrument pilot proficiency and training requirements
